en: The *Āgama Oral Explanation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*,
translated by the Anxi Upāsaka Duwei Anxuan and the Śramaṇa Yan Fotiao during the Later Han Dynasty.

Those who wish to sever the cycle of birth and death and attain the path that leads to transcendence of the world should contemplate and eliminate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

What are these twelve? First is fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*); second, from ignorance come volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); third, from volitional formations comes consciousness (*vijñāna*); fourth, from consciousness come name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); fifth, from name-and-form come the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); sixth, from the six sense bases comes contact (*sparśa*); seventh, from contact comes sensation (*vedanā*); eighth, from sensation comes craving (*tṛṣṇā*); ninth, from craving comes clinging (*upādāna*); tenth, from clinging comes becoming (*bhava*); eleventh, from becoming comes birth (*jāti*); twelfth, from birth come old age, sickness, death, and so forth. These are the matters of the twelve links of dependent origination.
When these twelve matters are about to arise, one should employ the four aspects of impermanence to extinguish them.
What are these four aspects of impermanence?
First is the recognition of suffering; second is the relinquishing of its origin; third is the knowledge of its cessation; and fourth is the practice of the Path.
Furthermore, it is said that one should contemplate birth, aging, illness, and death. By contemplating these four matters, one reverses the path of the twelve links of dependent origination.

A practitioner who contemplates these four matters and desires to transcend the world must sever the affairs of the twelve links of dependent origination; this constitutes the severing of the root of birth and death.
The twelve links of dependent origination have both internal and external aspects: first, internally it is ignorance (*avidyā*), externally it is earth;

second, internally it is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), externally it is water; third, internally it is consciousness (*vijñāna*), externally it is fire; fourth, internally it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), externally it is wind; fifth, internally it is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), externally it is space; sixth, internally it is affliction, externally it is the seed; seventh, internally it is sensation (*vedanā*), externally it is the root; eighth, internally it is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), externally it is the stem; ninth, internally it is grasping (*upādāna*), externally it is the leaf; tenth, internally it is becoming (*bhava*), externally it is the joint; eleventh, internally it is birth (*jāti*), externally it is the flower; twelfth, internally it is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), externally it is the fruit.
The birth and death of human beings arise from the twelve links of dependent origination internally; the birth and death of all things arise from the twelve links of dependent origination externally.
What is delusion (*moha*)?

It refers to failing to honor one’s parents, failing to distinguish between right and wrong, and because of these conditions, experiencing suffering that one does not wish to abandon, while having no faith in this world or the world beyond.

Once this has been done, there is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*); without this being done, it does not arise. Thus, when there is ignorance (*avidyā*), there is volitional formation; when there is volitional formation, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); when there is consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); when there is name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); when there are the six sense bases, there is contact (*sparśa*); when there is contact, there is feeling (*vedanā*); when there is feeling, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); when there is craving, there is grasping (*upādāna*); when there is grasping, there is becoming (*bhava*); when there is becoming, there is birth (*jāti*); and when there is birth, there is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Therefore, when human beings grasp at the twelve links of dependent origination, they undergo birth through these twelve links; without the conditions of dependent origination, there is no birth.
It is the same for all things.
As long as one does not sever the twelve links of dependent origination, one will not be liberated from birth and death.
One practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in order to attain the Way through them.
There are five matters within the twelve links of dependent origination:
the first is ignorance (*moha*).
Second is the essential activity of birth and death, which is the causal condition from previous lives;
third is consciousness, from which the body is received and born;
fourth is name-and-form, wherein the physical form further constitutes the five aggregates, which are the causal conditions of this present life.
Fifth, the six sense-fields (ṣaḍāyatana) further act as the seeds for the essential activity of birth and death; these are the causes and conditions for future lives.
Because they revolve through one another as causes and conditions across the three periods of time—past, present, and future—there are these five matters.
The twelve links of dependent origination fundamentally arise from the ten matters of the body, which in turn give rise to the ten matters.
Seven matters constitute one [link];
three matters proceed from four, thereby accomplishing seven matters.
The first consists of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech; these are grouped together as one based on form (*rūpa*).
Three matters are derived from four.
Envy, ill-will, and delusion arise from sensation, perception, mental formations, volitional formations, and consciousness.
These ten factors combined constitute the five aggregates, which then become the twelve links of dependent origination.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the name for the ground; when volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) flourish as the aggregates, one then performs the actions of birth and death.
The planting of one's own seeds is called "volitional formations.
Once there are volitional formations, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*) which undergoes the birth and death of taking up a body; once there is consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The body further performs ten things; once these are completed, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are formed. Once name-and-form (nāmarūpa) exists, there are the six sense bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana). These further produce the fullness of the aggregates; having planted the seeds of formations (saṃskāra), one shall subsequently undergo the cycle of transformation. Because this is the causal condition for birth and death, it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).

Regarding the ten matters of the body as the twelve links of dependent origination: envy is ignorance; hatred is birth-and-death; refined doubt is consciousness; killing is name-and-form; theft is the six sense bases; lust is contact; double-tongued speech is sensation; false speech is craving; harsh speech is becoming; and frivolous speech is existence. Because birth and existence are thus established, there are the twelve links of dependent origination.
Why is this? Lust is delusion, hatred is birth-and-death, and subtle doubt is consciousness; these three internal factors are the root.
Once these three factors exist, there are then seven factors, which constitute the five aggregates of clinging.
Because envy is the root of the five aggregates, it gives rise to doubt.

When the activities of the five aggregates encounter what is agreeable, one feels attachment; when encountering what is disagreeable, one feels aversion. This then produces the ten essential matters of birth and death, arising externally from the body and internally from the mind.
Doubt refers to failing to distinguish between white and black, and failing to recognize birth and death; therefore, it is for the sake of recognition.
A practitioner who wishes to sever the twelve links of dependent origination must first sever the ten matters of the body.
This is delusion; from delusion, the five aggregates cease, and the twelve links of dependent origination also cease.
Regarding the severance of the ten matters of the body: externally they proceed from the body and internally they proceed from the mind; therefore, they are called "body and mind."
"Upholding" means not killing.

It also refers to cutting off [evil] externally through the mouth and internally through jealousy. This means that when the mind does not give rise to thoughts regarding any of the myriad things, anger ceases; when anger ceases, killing ceases; when killing ceases, greed and desire cease; and when greed and desire cease, weeping ceases.
External speech refers to vocal sounds.
When vocal sounds are stilled, double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, and frivolous talk are likewise stilled.
Being free from doubt, one then enters the Way.
This is the returning [of the cycle] to sever the five aggregates and cut off the root of the twelve links of dependent origination.
There are three distinctions regarding the human reception of a body:
first, the flourishing aggregate of the five aggregates;
Second, the eighteen kinds;
third, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Through these three matters, one attains the three distinctions of the body.
First, regarding the "mass of the five aggregates" (*pañcaskandha-skandha*): the five aggregates arise from ten matters pertaining to the body.

From the eye comes the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); from the ear comes the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); from the nose comes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); from the mouth comes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and from the mind comes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
The mind takes mindfulness as its primary function; these six matters constitute the foundation. This is the ground of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Second, regarding the eighteen [elements], they enter into the nineteen faculties (*indriya*).

As for the eighteen kinds: the activity of the five aggregates constitutes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); that which possesses resistance and entry constitutes the basis of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
The six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute eighteen [elements] because consciousness (*vijñāna*) intervenes; thus they are nineteen faculties (*indriya*).
As for the statement that there are eighteen kinds, it is because consciousness does not arise [in certain cases], and thus they are eighteen kinds.
This explains that when the formations of the five aggregates flourish, eighteen kinds or nineteen faculties arise.
Third, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, these refer to the five aggregates.
Through the formations of the five flourishing aggregates, one seeks the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby possesses a body.
These are the ten matters concerning the same body, all of which are analyzed together.

From form (rūpa), one obtains the body; from the four aggregates (skandhas), one obtains name (nāman); from name-and-form (nāmarūpa), one obtains craving and sensation (vedanā); from sensation, one practices delusion (moha). Through the practice of delusion, the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) are thus formed.
The Way should be practiced for the sake of severance.
Form is not the body; it is merely a name that is called the body.
Although there are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, these too are not the body.
Why is this? If the ear were the person, it would be able to hear everything.
A name is derived from a physical form, just as, for example, the name "gold" is derived from the metal itself.
For example, when gold is fashioned into objects, it is by virtue of these forms that names are derived.
Earth, water, fire, wind, and space—these five elements compose the body, yet they are also not the body.
Why is this? It is because the body perceives smoothness; once a person has died, the earth no longer perceives smoothness.
One knows that earth, water, fire, wind, and space are not the body; the body is empty and the mind is also empty. Both being empty and non-existent, there is likewise no sensation or feeling.
Why is this? When a person has died, they no longer perceive pain or itching; thus, it is empty.
Once the mind has departed from the body, there is likewise no pain or itching; it is only because of the convergence of causes and conditions that [the body] returns to non-existence.
Within the body there are twelve winds:

the wind of upward-moving breath, the wind of downward-moving breath, the wind of the eyes, the wind of the ears, the wind of the nose, the wind of the back, the wind of the flanks, the wind of the navel, the wind of the arms, the wind of the feet, the wind of the joints, and the wind of the sword.
When the "sword-wind" reaches the patient, it is the sword-wind that kills living beings; the sword-wind severs the life-span of humans.
Regarding birth, old age, sickness, and death: "birth" refers to the moment one first descends into the mother's womb;
once born, one then ages.
"Stopping" refers to bringing the mind to rest.
By employing this stopping, one brings an end to the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
One clearly perceives that the body is fundamentally composed of ten factors that constitute its cessation.
Within the body there are five elements: first, earth; second, water; third, fire; fourth, wind; and fifth, space. That which is solid is earth;
that which is soft is water; that which is hot is fire; that which is movement is wind; and that through which food and drink pass in and out is space.
Furthermore, through the combination of other causes and conditions, one comes to be a human being and conceives of it as "this is my body.
If one desires [to understand] all things, one must examine and calculate the existence of this body.
There are also five causes and conditions that combine together:
First is form, second is sensation, third is perception, fourth is volitional formations, and fifth is consciousness.
When these ten factors combine, one perceives birth and death.
Matters are either good or evil.
There are two classes of those who practice goodness:
not transgressing the three [actions] of the body, the four of the mouth, and the three of the mind—this constitutes the first kind of goodness.
The two kinds of goodness are: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and freedom from doubt.
These are the two kinds of goodness.
Evil also has two classes:
Violating the three [precepts] of body, the four of speech, the three of mind, and drinking alcohol constitute the first evil;
doubt, envy, stinginess, and greed constitute the second evil.
Guarding body, speech, and mind constitutes the Way; the practitioner arises from merit.
From action one undergoes old age, sickness, and death, and the body then falls into decay.
When a person lies down and awakens, the mind departs from the body and rests upon the ground due to these causal conditions.
Why does one not die?
It is because the four conditions that sustain life have not yet dispersed.
When a person practices ten matters, they proceed toward three; when a person practices three matters, they proceed toward two; and when a person practices two matters, they proceed toward one.
What are the ten matters?
They are the ten unwholesome deeds, which result in the three matters of body, speech, and mind.
Once these three matters exist, there are then the two matters of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Once name-and-form (nāmarūpa) exists, one falls into delusion for a hundred kalpas; it is difficult to obtain a human birth with all faculties complete.

When a person is conceived, consciousness (vijñāna) acts as the seed upon the ground of semen. Although the consciousnesses of the five destinies have different names, they merge into a single consciousness; once this single consciousness enters [the womb], one loses what was originally known.
It is like a person born in the heavens: having received human consciousness, they take on celestial consciousness and thus forget all human affairs.
Humans arise from non-existence and die from existence.
For what reason does non-existence give rise to birth?
One does not know how there is birth from non-existence;
for what reason is there death?
One does not know how there is death from existence.
When consciousness does not arise again, one no longer dies; when consciousness exists, one no longer dies.
When the mind’s thoughts are extinguished, one immediately reaches the place of rebirth.
If the mental intentions are not extinguished, one cannot proceed to give rise to higher states of mind.
The mind arises and then ceases; one contemplates again, and though the thoughts are many, they must ultimately derive from the causal conditions received by the initial state of mind.
A person’s birth fundamentally originates from a woman; the body is obtained through the impurities and secretions of the husband and wife.

Having long since followed after evil associates, they are deceived by the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the twelve bases of cognition; consequently, there arise old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and suffering.
Birth and death constitute delusion; a person of wisdom should sever them.
The six bases of cessation are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
The twelve bases of decay are form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental desire.
To have a hidden thief within is the twelfth decay.
Human birth has three causes and conditions:
the first is conjunction.
The second is the aggregate;
the third is mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Sensation, perception, volition, becoming, and consciousness—these constitute the coming together.
All sensual desires constitute the aggregate.
Its upper part is the mind (*citta*), its middle is the intellect (*manas*), and its lower part is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
When a person first descends into the mother’s womb, they are like the yolk within a chicken egg.
By the thirty-seventh day, all parts—the head, face, hands, feet, and fingers—are fully formed;
four days before birth, the person is facing downward within the mother’s womb, experiencing unspeakable suffering.
While a person is in the mother’s womb, their life-force increases daily and their consciousness grows daily.
When the body gradually ages until the half-year mark, both the body and consciousness decrease daily.
To obtain a body is both a blessing and a source of transgression.
Why is this? Because obtaining a human body is a blessing, while hunger, thirst, cold, heat, lust, and envy are misdeeds.
There are five causes and conditions for a person to give birth to a child:
First, having a fundamental vow;
second, sharing common karma;
third, being proficient in ritual propriety.
Fourth is the coming of debts;
fifth is the repayment of debts.
What is meant by the original vow?
This refers to having seen a person’s son of handsome appearance in a previous life and then making a vow, saying:
"May my son be like this.
As for "fellow practitioners," it means those who, having engaged in the same calculations and deliberations, call one another by name upon obtaining profit.
"To understand propriety" means that one should treat each other with mutual respect and affection.
"The arrival of a debt" refers to the parents managing the household livelihood while the children use it recklessly.
"Repaying the debt" refers to the children managing the livelihood and handing over the proceeds to the parents; this is what constitutes repaying the debt.
A son is born due to three causes and conditions:
first, that the parents owed money to the son in a previous life;
second, that the son owed money to the parents in a previous life.
Third, an enemy comes to become one's son.
The parents toil and suffer to acquire wealth, yet they die before they can enjoy it; the son then takes possession and uses it. This is what is meant by the parents first being in debt to the son.
If a son goes out to seek wealth and property and dies immediately upon acquiring it, and his parents must use that which he earned, this is for the son to owe money to his parents.
Or, if a son dies after only a hundred days or a thousand days of life, leaving his parents in grief, sorrow, and distress, this is for enemies to follow one another from birth.
There are three types of sons born:
first, the son of merit;
second, the true son.
Third is the non-virtuous son.
What constitutes a virtuous son?
It refers to when the parents uphold the precepts, practice generosity, cultivate patience, and apply diligence in the path, and the son does likewise; this is called a virtuous son.
A "true child" refers to one whose parents do not believe in the Way, yet the child alone upholds the teachings of the Dao; this is a true child.

An "untrue child" refers to one whose parents follow the path of practice and act in accordance with the Dharma, while the child merely drinks wine and commits evil deeds, such that others find him loathsome to behold; this is an untrue child.
A child is born from his parents; there are those who share the same intentions, those who share the same conduct, and those who share the same thoughts.
To be long-lived, wealthy, noble, and handsome together is what is meant by "sharing the same conduct."
Covetousness and malice constitute a commonality of intent;
diligent practice of the Path constitutes a commonality of mindfulness.

If one’s original conduct was directed toward the father, one will mostly resemble the father; if one’s original conduct was directed toward the mother, one will mostly resemble the mother, because conduct that is not shared does not produce resemblance.

When a human being is born into this world, before they have yet acquired any knowledge, they instinctively reach out to their mother; this is due solely to the fundamental causes and conditions of their consciousness.

When a person comes into life, there are causes and conditions by which the body can pass through the space between [the womb and the world] without obstruction, yet after seven days, it begins to deteriorate once again.
There are also the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, but they are subtle and difficult to perceive.
When a person grows old and their consciousness becomes prone to forgetfulness, that consciousness gradually turns toward the place where it will be reborn.
Why is it that one does not know in advance the place where one will be born?
Because [the conditions] have not yet arrived.
One person gives birth to another, one person comes to the place of another, and one person grieves for another; this is because of long-standing habitual practice from time immemorial.
One who does not study [this] finds that the body has three kinds of suffering, and the mind likewise has three kinds of suffering.
As for the suffering of the body, it refers to being struck by knives, staves, tiles, or stones, or being kicked and trampled;
the second is illness and emaciation.
Third is death.
Regarding mental suffering: first, it is the grief for one's parents, siblings, wife, children, and acquaintances;
second, it is the grief for wealth, treasures, and enemies.
For what reason is there suffering?
It is said that suffering arises because the five aggregates are unbalanced.
For what reason is there the aggregate of death?
Because it has matured and decayed, it is called death.
All illnesses are produced by the mind; the body itself has no cognition, and therefore it does not create these illnesses.
For what reason, then, does this body become ill?
Because the four causal conditions are unequal,
why would there be sorrow?
It is because everything is contrary to one's wishes.
Why is it not fixed?
Because the illness has passed away.
Why is it urgent?
One wishes to destroy it.
Why? Because it is shattered by the poison of bodily decay.
Why is it called old age and death?
Because of decay.
Why is it called impermanent?
Because one lacks autonomy,
why is it suffering?
Because it is urgent.
Why is it empty?
Because there is no master.
What does it mean to say "I act"?
Thinking that what is not the self cannot be separated from suffering nor can it experience suffering—these are the ten matters.
There are generally three things that people desire; those things loved by people, they always wish to obtain.
First, physical vigor;
second, peace and security;
third, longevity.
Furthermore, there are three more enemies:
first, old age, which is the enemy of physical vigor;
second, illness, which is the enemy of well-being.
Third, the death of the body is the enemy of longevity. There are also three refuges:
first, taking refuge in the Buddha; [the second is taking refuge in the Dharma; the third is taking refuge in the Sangha].
Second is taking refuge in the Dharma;
third is taking refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus.
There are four things that are to be feared:
First is birth;
second is aging;
third is illness;
The fourth is death.
There are five causes and conditions for a person’s face to turn red:
the first is being near fire.
Second is drinking alcohol;
third is fear;
fourth is harboring anger.
Fifth, one has much shame and remorse.
There are four causes and conditions for the hair turning white:
first, an excess of fire; [the rest as per the source].
Second, much sorrow;
third, much illness;
fourth, early graying of the hair.
There are four causes and conditions for a person to become ill and emaciated:
first, eating little;
second, having sorrow.
Third, being prone to excessive sorrow;
fourth, having an ill body that is not yet harmonized.
There are four matters that one should not disclose to others beforehand:
First, the hair turns white;
second, old age;
third, illness.
Fourth is death.
These four matters cannot be avoided, nor can they be escaped, nor can they be repelled.
There are four matters that cannot be endured:
First is hunger;
second is thirst;
third is cold.
Fourth is heat.
Furthermore, the body has four conditions:
first, insufficiency; [and so forth].
Second, not being full;
third, not being satiated;
fourth, not being weary of it.
Furthermore, the body has four kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering at the time of birth; second, the suffering at the time of old age; [third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of death].
Third is the pain of illness;
fourth is the pain of death.
All tastes do not exceed eight kinds:
First, bitter;
second, astringent;
third, pungent.
Fourth, salty;
fifth, bland;
sixth, sweet;
Seventh is sour;
eighth is indistinct flavor.

An increase in bitterness augments cold and heat; an excess of astringency augments wind and dispels cold; pungent flavors dispel water [phlegm]; sour flavors dispel wind but cause the eyes to grow dim.
There are three causes and conditions by which food enters the marrow and the blood vessels:
first, fatty richness; second, poison;
[and third, the heat of digestion].
Third is alcohol.
These three [substances] pervade the entire body, reaching every part without exception.
All that is eaten and drunk contains some degree of fat and grease; there is only a difference in their thinness or thickness, and their quantity or scarcity.
There are four kinds of people:
first, those of the householder class;
second, those of the path-and-arts class.
Third, the class of shamans;
fourth, the class of farmers.
There are four types of birth:
First, birth from a womb;
second, birth from the union of cold and heat;
third, miraculous birth.
The fourth is birth from an egg.
Birth from a womb refers to humans and animals.
Birth from moisture produced by the blending of cold and heat refers to insects, moths, fleas, and lice.
Those born by transformation (upapāduka) refer to the devas and those in the hells.
Those born from eggs (aṇḍaja) refer to birds, fish, and turtles.
A human head consists of forty-five bones; from the waist upward there are fifty-one bones, and the four limbs consist of one hundred and four bones, totaling two hundred bones.
The human body has seven hundred thousand channels and nine million nine hundred thousand pores; one who attains contemplation can see them all clearly and distinguish them individually.
There are Arhats who, using their divine eye to see through all things, observe that there are very many women falling into the hells.
He then asked the Buddha,
"For what reason?
The Buddha said:
"It is due to four causes and conditions:
first, because of greed for precious objects, clothing, and bedding, desiring to obtain much;
second, because of mutual jealousy."
Third, they engage in much idle chatter;
fourth, they assume seductive postures and are excessively lustful.
For these reasons, they fall into hell in great numbers.
The Oral Explanation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination from the Āgamas.
